fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a Science Quiz
fields.features_subheading: A science quiz tests what someone knows about the natural world. Emergent builds the questions and the scoring from a prompt.
fields.feature_1:
Questions tagged by strand

Name the unit and grade, such as 8th-grade forces, and Emergent writes each question with one right option and three wrong ones. Each is tagged life, physical, or earth science.
fields.feature_2:
A reason and a source under each answer

Give each question a one-line explanation and a source link. The results screen shows both after the last answer, so a student who disputes a point can check the page.
fields.feature_3:
Every answer saved as a row

Each answer lands in a database you own, stored with the player, the question, and its strand. Sort the table by question to find the one a class keeps getting wrong.
fields.feature_4:
One question per phone screen

Players see one question at a time, so a 10-year-old in a museum hall can finish on a phone without zooming in. Emergent puts no cap on how many people take the quiz.
fields.feature_5:
A pass mark that triggers an email

Set a pass mark, such as 10 of 10 on a lab rules quiz, and the app emails the teacher each student below it. Send the alert to a Slack channel when a department needs it.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain and the full code

Run the quiz on a school domain; custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits. Paid plans export the full code to your GitHub repository for a developer to extend.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Science Quizzes, Four Different Jobs
fields.tab_content_1:
Students under 10 of 10 retake before the first lab

Before anyone at Harlow Ridge High School lights a burner, all 112 chemistry students take a 10-question lab rules quiz on their phones. The pass mark is 10 of 10. This fall, 14 students fell short, and Tamsin Doyle, who teaches all 4 sections, got an email naming each one. All 14 retook the quiz before Thursday's first lab.
fields.tab_content_2:
The hottest planet question was missed in 702 plays

Kids visiting the planet hall at the Halvorsen Science Center open a 12-question space quiz from a sign by the door and answer one question per screen. October brought 1,240 plays. The question on which planet is hottest was missed in 702 of them, more than any other. Staff then put a card next to the Venus model.
fields.tab_content_3:
Of the 3 strands, physical science gained least

The 38 students at the Sutter Pines Homeschool Co-op take the same 15 questions in September and again in May, 5 per strand. Every answer is saved with its strand. The average rose to 11.2 of 15, up from 6.8. Physical science rose just 1.3 points, the smallest gain of the 3 strands. Next fall opens with a physics unit.
fields.tab_content_4:
96 campers land in 3 groups by score

Elkmont STEM Camp gives campers aged 9 to 12 a 12-question placement quiz. A score of 10 or more goes to Lab Crew, 6 to 9 to Builders, and 5 or under to Explorers. This summer, 23 of the 96 campers went to Lab Crew, 42 to Builders, and 31 to Explorers. The director, Ingrid Paulsen, gets each roster by email.

plan.angle: The top 10 is all play: Britannica, Sporcle, Pew Research, BuzzFeed, ScienceQuiz.net and Science Fun for kids offer science quizzes to take, and none shows how to make one with your own questions and see the answers. This page gives the searcher both: an 8-question science quiz on planets, cells, the body, and forces to play on the page, each answer sourced to NASA, NIH, or MedlinePlus, then four science quizzes a high school, a science center, a homeschool co-op, and a summer camp run as their own app, with every answer saved to a table they own.
tab_stories: At Harlow Ridge High School, 112 chemistry students take a 10-question lab rules quiz and need 10 of 10 before their first lab; 14 fall short, teacher Tamsin Doyle gets an email naming them, and they retake it before Thursday.

The Halvorsen Science Center puts a 12-question space quiz for kids on visitors' phones in its planet hall, logs 1,240 plays in October, and finds the hottest planet question missed in 702 of them, so staff add a sign next to the Venus model.

The Sutter Pines Homeschool Co-op gives its 38 students the same 15-question quiz in September and May, and the average rises from 6.8 to 11.2 of 15, with physical science gaining the least, so next fall opens with a physics unit.

Elkmont STEM Camp has 96 campers aged 9 to 12 take a 12-question placement quiz at sign-up, and the score bands sort them into Explorers, Builders, and Lab Crew, with the 3 rosters emailed to director Ingrid Paulsen.
